provenance.citation: Weizenbaum, J. (1966). ELIZA—A computer program for the study of natural language communication between man and machine. Communications of the ACM, 9(1), 36–45. https://doi.org/10.1145/365153.365168
provenance.locus: Opening dialogue (p. 36), decomposition/reassembly mechanics (pp. 37–40), and Appendix "An ELIZA Script" (pp. 44–45) — DOCTOR script rules: ALIKE/DIT (rank 10), ALWAYS (rank 1), MY=YOUR (rank 2) with /FAMILY tag, I keyword (sad/unhappy/depressed pattern), REMEMBER (rank 5), DREAMT (rank 4), IF, MEMORY MY
provenance.notes: The existing realElizaInput() is a stub — intent-only with no rules, facts, goals, or state. The improved fixture encodes: (1) the six opening utterances from the verbatim dialogue on p. 36, as facts keyed by utterance index; (2) all keyword/decomposition/reassembly rules directly from the Appendix script (pp. 44–45) covering ALIKE→DIT, ALWAYS, MY/FAMILY, I+depressed, I+want/need, REMEMBER, DREAMT, IF, MEMORY MY, NONE, YOU patterns; (3) goals capturing the two core ELIZA objectives: detect dominant theme and reflect back via keyword decomposition; (4) state atoms encoding the DOCTOR script name, the unconditional pronoun swap rule (I↔YOU, MY↔YOUR, ME↔YOU cited explicitly on p. 37), and the left-to-right highest-rank-wins scan rule. The decomposition notation (0 K 0) and reassembly slot numbering (component 3/4/5) are verbatim from the paper. The opening 3-turn dialogue exchange is the canonical worked example Weizenbaum presents on p. 36 to introduce the system.

facts.value: They're always bugging us about something or other.

He says I'm depressed much of the time.
I need some help, that much seems certain.
